title: Efficient Inference on High-Dimensional Linear Models With Missing Outcomes: consistency of the dual solution with an estimated propensity score
author: Yikun Zhang, Alexander Giessing, Yen-Chi Chen
work: Efficient Inference on High-Dimensional Linear Models With Missing Outcomes
difficulty_reason: Counted unit: the article's Theorem (source0.tex lines 562--574, source label thm:dual_consist2), the paper's headline consistency result for the dual solution of the debiasing program: under the article's five standing assumptions plus an explicit growth condition on the sparsity, the sample size, the confidence level and the propensity-score rate, and under an explicit upper bound on the approximation parameter, the computed dual solution approximates the sparse population dual solution with a stated rate and probability at least one minus delta; delivered with the article's complete original proof (source0.tex lines 2620--2713, one appendix proof environment of 94 lines whose heading names the counted theorem). The proof is complete and closed inside the retained span together with its retained context. It starts from the optimality inequality of the estimated dual program, differentiates it into a quadratic inequality, decomposes that inequality into the corresponding deterministic-propensity inequality plus three error terms that isolate the effect of the estimated propensity scores, bounds the right-hand side by Hoelder's inequality and the cone/ball geometry of the sparse approximation, bounds the three error terms through the retained auxiliary results on restricted eigenvalues, cone-ball unions, cross-polynomial remainder terms and the rate of the propensity-score estimate, combines them into a quadratic inequality for the deviation, and finally extracts the stated rate by substituting the growth condition. Every quoted auxiliary result is delivered as a retained statement, and the counted proof is self-contained modulo those statements. H2: a research-level high-dimensional statistics theorem whose proof combines empirical-process concentration, cone and restricted-eigenvalue geometry and a plug-in propensity-score error decomposition; the argument and its rate conditions are well beyond ordinary PhD qualifying exercises.
